Issued at 155 PM CDT Thu Oct 29 2026

Early afternoon analysis showed yesterday's cold front now 
stretching from northeast MO toward southwest KS. Behind the front, 
surface ridging was leading to quiet weather with plenty of sunshine 
across the area. Temperatures as of 1 PM were mostly in the 60s,
with perhaps a few 70 degree readings in southeast NE.

The quiet weather will be short-lived, however, as the front to our 
south starts to advance back northward as a warm front this evening. 
In addition, warm air advection and low level transport will be 
ramping up, leading to shower and isolated non-severe thunderstorm 
development north of the front by late evening into the overnight 
hours. Accumulation should generally remain southeast of a line from 
Norfolk to Sioux City. Any notable north of I-80 should gradually 
diminish through the day, though some light spotty showers or even 
some drizzle could linger in these areas. To the south, guidance 
suggests ongoing potential for showers and a few isolated storms 
lingering into early afternoon before we see a brief lull from mid 
to late afternoon. Precip redevelopment should then occur by early 
evening (around 6 PM) as shortwave energy currently along the 
TX/Mexico border pushes into the area and the surface warm front 
starts to slide farther north into the forecast area. Given the 
cloud cover and precip during the day, instability will be limited, 
but guidance does show some elevated instability sneaking in behind 
the front, which would be just enough for some additional 
thunderstorm threat. Severe weather is not expected, but you'll want 
to keep an eye on the weather if you have outdoor plans Friday 
night.

Like Friday, Saturday will see some lingering light showers during 
the day, but the general trend throughout the day will be to dry 
out, with 30-40% chances in the morning giving way to 15-20% chances 
for the afternoon and evening. Outside of the precip, it is looking 
like a fairly nice Halloween, with high temperatures mostly in the 
60s and evening temperatures in the upper 50s to lower 60s with a 
light south to southeast breeze. Some additional shortwave energy 
will slide in late Saturday night into early Sunday and bring 
additional spotty showers, but shouldn't amount to too much.

Attention then turns to a much stronger system progged to move 
through the area Monday and Tuesday, possibly into Wednesday. The 
general idea is that a cutoff low currently spinning off the Pacific 
Northwest coast will move into the Desert Southwest and phase up 
with a trough currently well off into the Pacific. A fairly strong 
surface low will develop east of the Rockies and track across the 
Plains through the middle part of the week, bringing widespread 
precipitation to the area. The main questions remain track and 
timing/speed of the system, with solutions ranging from precip 
ending late Monday night/early Tuesday to precip ending late 
Wednesday night. Some ensemble members also suggest a decent plume 
of instability out ahead of the system, which could yield at least a 
small severe storm threat given the amount of shear that usually 
accompanies these systems. In addition, NAEFS guidance suggests 
precipitable water values approaching or exceeding 1.5", which is in 
the 99th+ percentile of climatology for this time of year, so the 
rain would likely be pretty efficient. Finally, it will also likely 
be pretty gusty at times as the system moves through, with ensembles 
showing 30-40 mph gusts ahead of and behind the low. Otherwise, 
expect high temperatures to remain in the 60s and 70s through Monday 
before the northwesterly flow on the back side starts to usher in 
cooler air and highs fall into the 50s and 60s.
